ATTACKED WHEN ALMOST HOME.
HOW A ROSLYN MERCHANT WAS ROBBED.
WILLIAM M. VALENTINE KNOCKED DOWN AND PROBABLY FATALLY BEATEN—THE ROBBERS ONLY PARTLY SUCCESSFUL.

William M. Valentine, one of the oldest, wealthiest and most respected merchants of Roslyn, L. I., started from his store, which is on the main street of the village, on Tuesday night at 9:10 o'clock to go to his home. His favorite method of reaching home was to row across what is called the grist mill pond, which lies directly behind his store. The landing place on the other side of the pond is at the foot of a little hill upon his own grounds and within twenty yards of his house. On the night mentioned he did not reach home at the usual hour, and his wife grew restless waiting for him. She placed lights in the window to attract his attention, but still he did not come. Dreading lest something should have happened to him, she ran to a neighbor, Justice Losee, and told him of her fears for her husband.

The Justice immediately started to the boat landing, and at the brow of the hill, within a few yards of the landing, and within twenty rods of his home, he discovered the inanimate form of Mr. Valentine, lying wounded and bleeding under a large evergreen bush. Assistance was speedily summoned, and the wounded man was conveyed to his house. The druggist of the village, Mr. Hooper, and Mr. Valentine's family physician, Dr. Bogart, were sent for, and quickly responded to the call. Mr. Valentine's skull was found fractured, with a cut in it three inches long and an inch and a quarter wide. Mr. Valentine continued unconscious all day yesterday and was unable to give an account of the assault upon him. When he left the store, he had in his possession between $300 and $400. Twelve dollars had been taken from him, which was in an outside pocket. The remainder was in an inside breast pocket, and, together with his watch, was untouched.

A careful search was made at the scene of the robbery, and the footprints of two men were found, the tracks showing plainly in the soft mud, leading in an easterly direction across a ploughed field. Some of the tracks were made by rubber boots. A large stud stick, covered with blood, was found close to the evergreen bush. There was a pool of blood where Mr. Valentine was discovered. The boat was found tied to the moorings at the foot of the hill, showing that Mr. Valentine had landed and was proceeding to the house when attacked. Sheriff Wright, of Queens County, with the assistance of a New-York detective, endeavored to find a clew to the robbers. Edward Alberson, a negro, was arrested yesterday, and held. He is a wandering vagabond, wears rubber boots, and his foot is said to fit one of the tracks exactly. Joseph Bennett, a boy of nineteen, who has a bad reputation, was also arrested, but was subsequently released. The officers think that they will succeed in finding the guilty persons.

Dr. Hoag, of Manhassett, and Dr. Hendrickson, of Jamaica, who were summoned to attend the wounded man, state that there is little or no hope of his recovery. He is seventy-three years old. His wife and one son constitute his family. He has many relatives in the neighborhood. It is thought that the highwaymen were frightened away by the lights Mrs. Valentine placed in the window before they had succeeded in rifling the body of their victim and thus failed to secure the large amount of money, which Mr. Valentine had with him. Mr. Valentine is estimated to be worth $80,000. He was born in Roslyn. It has been his habit for some time to row across the pond from the store to his home, often carrying large sums of money. It is to this well-known habit that the assault upon him is attributed. At a meeting held by his neighbors it was decided to offer a reward for the arrest and conviction of Mr. Valentine's assaults. The weapon with which the crime was committed is a short stick from a market wagon.

THE ASSAULT ON MR. VALENTINE.
THE ASSAULT ON MR. VALENTINE.

The condition of William M. Valentine, the aged merchant of Roslyn, L. L., who was beaten and robbed on Tuesday night in his own yard, continued unchanged yesterday, and he was unable to tell any of the circumstances of the assault upon him. Detective James Ayres was busy yesterday trying to discover who were the persons concerned in the crime. No doubt is entertained of the guilt of Edward Alberson, the negro who was locked up on Wednesday. His rubber boot, even to the welt on the sole, fits exactly in the deep tracks that were left in the ploughed ground. Alberson had worked for Mr. Valentine and was discharged a short time ago, because of his worthlessness. On Tuesday he endeavored to obtain some tobacco at the store on credit, but Mr. Valentine refused to let him have it. On Wednesday morning Alberson was seen in company with a young negro named James Eto, who also earns an uncertain livelihood by doing little jobs about the village, and who has recently served a term in the State Prison. The two negroes walked past Mr. Valentine's store in the forenoon and asked carelessly why the store was closed, although everyone in the village had been talking about the robbery.

Detective Ayres tried to find Eto yesterday, but he had disappeared, and, a vigorous search being unavailing, the detective, in company with James Valentine, the son of the injured man, came to New-York in the afternoon, as it was supposed that Eto had fled there after the arrest of Alberson. Young Mr. Valentine says that he has no doubt of the guilt of these two negroes, as their evil reputation and the knowledge which they had of the habit of his father in coming home late at night, together with the evidence furnished by the footprints, point conclusively to them as the assailants of his father. The stories told by Alberson of his movements at the time when the crime was committed were found to be false. This is the second time he has been in the hands of the law. Three years ago he was arrested for barn burning near Flushing, but he charged the crime upon his father, who was locked up, and who committed suicide in jail pending the trial. The sum of $800 was subscribed at the meeting Wednesday night as a reward for the conviction of Mr. Valentine's assailants.

MR. VALENTINE'S SUPPOSED ASSAILANTS.
Officer James Ayres on Thursday evening arrested James Eato, the negro who is suspected of being one of the persons who assaulted Mr. Valentine, the aged merchant of Roslyn, L. I., on Tuesday night. District-Attorney Downing, of Queens County, was informed and went immediately to Roslyn. Edward Aloerson, the negro who had been arrested the day before, and Eato, were arraigned before Justice Losce. Three witnesses testified that the two negroes were together in Joyce's liquor store on Tuesday evening until 9 o'clock. At that time they left the store together and did not return. The negroes claimed to have been at their homes at the time the assault was committed. Justice Losce committed them to the lockup to await the result of Mr. Valentine's injuries.

Yesterday placards offering a reward of $450 for the arrest and conviction of the persons guilty of the assault were posted in the village. Colonel Aaron A. Degrauw, of Jamaica, a wealthy relative of Mr. Valentine, who is directing the search, and Deputy Sheriff Charles Hance were in Roslyn. Eato's shoes were found to fit exactly the second set of tracks in the ploughed ground. Eato is a married man and has two children. He says that he had not worn the shoes for a week, and on Wednesday morning he found them in his house after a long search and took them to the village shoemaker to be repaired. The statement that he was home at 9:30 o'clock is contradicted by that of his wife, and yesterday afternoon the officers said that they could prove that the two negroes were seen within a hundred yards of the spot where Mr. Valentine was robbed, within ten minutes of the time the assault was perpetrated. Another circumstance tending to convict Eato is that he is left-handed, and the nature of the blow on Mr. Valentine's head shows that it was probably done by a left-handed person. Thursday night Officer Hance secreted himself near the lock-up, where the negroes are confined, and listened for what they might say; but they kept unbroken silence throughout the night. They will be taken to the County Jail to-day.

Mr. Valentine remained yesterday in an unconscious condition. Plaster casts have been taken of the footprints. A diligent search has been made for the pocketbook containing $10 which was taken from the merchant by the robbers, but it has not been found. Mr. Valentine had $300 in an inside pocket which he intended bringing to New-York on the next day to pay some bills; this the thieves in their hurry overlooked.

REMOVED TO THE QUEENS COUNTY JAIL.
William Valentine, of Roslyn, L. L., who was attacked by robbers on Tuesday night, was so much better yesterday that he inquired as to the health of several of his old friends who are ill. His physician, however, refused to allow him to converse. There is some fear that he will lose his eyesight. He is partly paralyzed in the left side, and he can only distinguish people by their voices. The two prisoners, Alberson and Eato, were removed to the Queens County Jail in Long Island City last night. A crowd gathered at the Roslyn depot when they left and threatened to lynch them. The Sheriff's officers had great difficulty in getting the men on the cars in safety. A heavy bail-cloak, with blood stains upon it, has been found hidden in Eato's house, but he denies any knowledge of it. The Sheriff, however, has strong proof that it belongs to him.

THE ROSLYN ROBBERY CONFESSED.

Since the arrest of the colored men, Edward Albertson and James Eato, on the charge of assaulting and robbing William M. Valentine, at Roslyn, on March 21, they have been kept confined in separate cells in the Queens County Jail, and no persons excepting Deputy Sheriffs Hanse and Ayers, who have been assiduously at work on the case, have been allowed to converse with them. Yesterday morning the two deputies visited Eato in his cell. After a few minutes's conversation the prisoner broke down completely and confessed the entire story to the officers. Eato said that Albertson, who is his cousin, had talked to him several times about robbing Mr. Valentine, while he was on his way home, but he at first refused to have anything to do with the project. Finally Albertson overcame his scruples and he agreed to go with him. It was agreed that they should meet near the railroad depot the first dark and stormy night, go to the grounds surrounding Mr. Valentine's house, and wait for his arrival. They examined the ground, and concluded that the best spot to secrete themselves was behind the evergreen tree near the place where Mr. Valentine's body was found. It was decided that the robbery should be effected as the old gentleman came up from the pond on his way to the house.

On the night of the assault and robbery the two proceeded to the spot described, and took up their positions behind the tree. Albertson had previously cut a club from a piece of wood he picked up on the roadway. They had only been hidden a few moments when they heard Mr. Valentine tying up his boat on the shore of the pond. An instant later and the old gentleman passed the tree at a brisk pace. Albertson crept up behind him, and dealt him a terrible blow on the head. Eato says Mr. Valentine fell to the ground like a log. Almost at the moment the blow was struck a light was seen moving in one of the front windows of the house, which was only a short distance from where they stood. Fearing detection they fled, not having time to rifle Mr. Valentine's clothing, except the pocket that contained the money they stole. To corroborate his story Eato was taken to Roslyn yesterday afternoon. Upon reaching his home, Eato took the officers into the cellar, and removed a stone from the foundation. THE GOOD AND ILL-LUCK OF TWO MEN.
THE GOOD AND ILL-LUCK OF TWO MEN.

James Eato, the colored man, who on Wednesday confessed to complicity to the assault and robbery of Mr. Valentine, at Roslyn, L. L., has made an additional statement, implicating a third person, whose name is withheld by the officers, as he has not yet been arrested. There will be no further examination before the Justice, as it is considered by the prosecuting officers of the county that the confession of Eato and the recovery of the stolen property at his house are sufficient to justify the Grand Jury in indicting the two prisoners now in custody. Mr. Valentine's condition is comparatively unchanged. He lies most of the time in a comatose state, but occasionally he is conscious. In one of these periods his son questioned him. He said that he came home by the boat, entered his house, walked into the kitchen and had a smoke before going to bed. He did not express any knowledge of having been injured.

Eato has also confessed the particulars of a plot between himself, Albertson and the man who has not yet been arrested to rob the agent of the Long Island Railroad Company at Roslyn. They lay in wait for him on the night of the assault upon Mr. Valentine, but he went home by a different road. Eato says that it was this disappointment that caused them to agree to attack Mr. Valentine.

Bedford.—John Carson, age forty-seven, a carpenter, hung himself with a sash cord in an unfinished house on James Sutton's place between Mt. Kisco and the Village of Bedford, about 6 o'clock yesterday morning. He had been foreman for Mr. Sutton during the past two years. It is supposed that his perplexity over the planning of the new house, which is of a very peculiar style of construction, had led him to commit the act.

White Plains.—In the Surrogate's Court at White Plains yesterday witnesses were examined for the executors in the contested will case of Miss Sarah Merritt, of Port Chester. Jared V. Peck, one of the subscribing witnesses to the will, testified to the circumstances under which the will was prepared by Stephen H. Thayer, and the condition of the testator's mind at the time it was executed. He also testified that he considered that Miss Merritt was quite competent to make a will and that she was under no restraint.

WHITESTONE.—About 5 o'clock on Sunday afternoon a siop-yacht, believed to hail from Greenpoint, with a party of twenty or more people on board, appeared in the offing at Whitestone. They cut loose and sailed away with several row-boats that were fastened to a United States revenue cutter. No trace of the boats or the men who took them has been discovered. The property stolen is valued at over $500.

LONG ISLAND CITY.—The difficulty between the Common Council of Long Island City and the local Board of Education promises to develop into a serious complication. The Aldermen appointed an expert to examine the books of the School Commissioners, and when President Gleason demanded the books in behalf of the city he was met by a refusal. The Aldermen are about to take the matter before the courts. The trial of James Eato and Edward Albertson, the two negroes charged with assaulting and robbing Mr. William E. Valentine, at Roslyn, last April, began at the Queens County Court of Sessions, in Long Island City, yesterday, before Judge John J. Armstrong and Associate Justices Clowes and Lawrence. Eato was defended by George A. Mott and Albertson by William J. Stanford. The counsel for Eato requested that his client should be tried separately, and the Court granted the application. Eato pleaded not guilty. Only eight jurymen were obtained, when the panel of forty-eight was exhausted. Judge Armstrong ordered an additional panel of seventy-five, and adjourned the court until te-day.

The Story of a Crime.
Southern Indiana is the scene of one of the most horrible murders in the history of that state, and the details are given by the confession of the assassin, his mother and brother, who are all safely lodged in the county jail at Richmond. David H. Smith, an aged farmer who lived near Richmond, was killed Jan. 16th by his son Daniel, and his body was found a few days after under 19 feet of water in an abandoned well near his house. It appears that there had long been a feud between the old man and his wife and sons. Not long ago Dan traded one of his father's horses without his knowledge, and a dispute followed which so enraged the son that he laid deliberate plans, in which he was undoubtedly aided by his mother and brother, to get the old man out of the way. According to his story, he followed him into the yard and, with a revolver which he had calmly put in perfect order for his bloody work, shot him three times in quick succession, and then, dragging him dead to the unused well, threw him in. Mrs. Smith says that Dan called to her as soon as he had shot, asking her to help him drag the dead man away, but, she says indifferently, "I refused to help him." The murderer's brother, Jake, says that he was cutting wood at the time of the murder and did not know of it until Dan said with an oath, "I've shot him and put him in the well and he'll never bother us any more." Smith was soon missed by his acquaintances, and, as the family troubles were well known and Dan had publicly threatened to kill his father, foul play was at once suspected and a large party of men went with officers to search the premises. The family answered questions evasively and tried to appear indifferent while the party, dividing the search, examined the house and out-buildings, until the well was sounded and the old man's decaying body found. When it was raised to the surface the wife and sons feigned grief and surprise; but their attempts were of no avail, and the next day they confessed. Not long before his murder Smith told a lawyer the sad story of his life at home. A painracked, infirm old man, he had been abused in all conceivable ways by his wife and children. The whole story of his life and death would scarcely be credited if it was not officially told. The community in which he lived is still excited over the crime, and his unnatural son narrowly escaped lynching.

DEED OF A DEMON
HORRIBLE CRIME COMMITTED BY A MINNEAPOLIS BRUTE.
He Entices Away and Ravishes a Little Girl, 4 Years Old—Particulars of the Inhuman Affairs—Intense Excitement in Minneapolis—Fears of Lynching.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]
INTEGRALS April 27. One of the
MINNEAPOLIS, April 27.—One of the most dastardly, hellish deeds in the whole category of crimes was committed in this city late yesterday afternoon, the particulars of which, as gathered by a GLOBE reporter, are as follows:

Minnie Little, a 4 year old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jason P. Spear, residing at 1,016 Fourth avenue south, an unusually bright, pretty child, was permitted to go to a neighboring confectionery store on Eleventh street. While there she was accosted by a young man who purchased a small quantity of sweet-meats. He then induced her to take a little walk with him, saying he would go with her to a better store where he would buy lots of nice things.

They had not been gone long before her delayed return home was noted by the anxious mother, who at once instituted a search. At the store she learned the appaling intelligence of the child's departure under the suspicious condition's mentioned. The nearly distracted mother gave the alarm throughout the neighborhood. Search for the decoyed child was general. Meanwhile, a request for a policeman to be sent post haste was sent to headquarters. Officer Gleason was detailed for the duty. While he did not know the nature of the errand he realized the fact that he should exercise all the expedition possible. Consequently he confiscated the first horse and drove hurriedly out to Fourth avenue south.

By this time the man who had induced the little girl to go with him, had compassed his nefarious designs and was returning. Arriving in front of the residence of Geo. Smith, Mrs. Smith recognized the fiend, and hailing him, asked where her girl was. He only replied with curses and abuses. At this juncture the officer came dashing up the street. The wretch recognizing the policeman's star and brass buttons, started with all possible speed across the vacant block adjoining Capt. Snyder's residence on Tenth street. He was soon run down, however, and subsequently turned over to Chief Munger at the station.

An examination of the prisoner by Chief Munger, resulted in the discovery of almost certain evidences of his crime about the person.

Half an hour after the deed was committed, the child was found near Third and a half avenue and Seventh street in the bushes, in a horrible condition, bleeding profusely and nearly unconscious. She was taken home and three physicians, Drs. Abbott, Wells and French, were summoned. After examination and consultation, they pronounced the girl in a critical condition, and her recovery is considered doubtful.

The parents are beside themselves with grief and indignation. The wildest exultement prevails throughout the city. The parents are highly respected and enjoy the friendship of a large circle.

Lynching is threatened, but to guard against such an occurrence Chief Munger has issued special orders to the police to use extra vigilance and caution. No one is admitted to see the prisoner from a fear that he might be shot on the spot.

The prisoner gave his name one time as Frank, at another as John McManniss. He is apparently about 26, of medium height, heavily built, with a heavy sandy mustache, an ugly scar on his left cheek extending nearly to the point of the chin, and another scar on the right side of his face. He is dressed in a Scotch suit and looks like a railroad employee. He claims to hail from Boston. He has been in the city only a few weeks and has worked at carpentering.

It is generally believed from the description of the person that he is the same who assaulted a lady in Oak Lake addition two weeks since. He exultantly acknowledged his guilt to Officer Bates.

EXCITEMENT ON THE INCREASE.
At 11 o'clock scores of excited citizens were to be seen at various localities and on the street corners, and the mayor, to insure the safety and protection of the prisoner, had him surreptitiously conveyed to the county jail. The excitement at 1 o'clock is increasing.

LATEST.
The latest from the scene of excitement in Minneapolis is that the crowd after filling the streets for several hours gave up any idea of lynching the dastard on account of a report which gradually gained credence that the prisoner had been spirited away in some manner by the officers of the law who feared the crowd would break the jail open.

A Wretch Strung Up.
ST. PAUL, April 28. —About one o'clock this morning a party of masked men appeared at the jail in Minneapolis, and demanded the surrender of Frank McManus, a tramp who ravished and cruelly mutilated a four year old child, Nina Spear, yesterday. The Sheriff was made a prisoner by the mob but refused to divulge the whereabouts of McManus. The mob then made a thorough search of the jail, breaking open every cell on the first floor without finding the prisoner. They then ascended to the floor above, and repeated the ceremony of breaking open the cell doors, until McManus was found. The latter was taken to the house of his victim, where he was fully identified. Without further ceremony he was taken to a tree in front of the High School building and hanged him high from a limb, at 4:15 this morning. Before McManus was strung up he confessed his horrible crime. He was a tramp, 26 years old, and came from Boston. Excitement ran very high during the night both in Minneapolis and St. Paul, and public sentiment is indisputedly with the men who thus administered justice to another one of the most atrocious crimes in the annals of Minnesota. The child victim is in a precarious condition, and there is little chance of her recovery.

Frank McManus, aged 26, claiming to hail from Boston, coaxed the four year old daughter of Jason P. Spear into the suburbs, where he outraged and horribly mutilated her so that she will probably die. The message sent Congress by the President calls attention to the necessity of prompt repressive measures in regard to the Cow-boy disturbances in Arizona which have gained such headway as to require a resort to extraordinary remedies in view of the inability of the civil authorities to restore order. The President suggests the use of a part of the army as a posse comitatus, and recommends the passage of an enabling measure with this end in view.

WASHINGTON, D. C., April 28. — The House resolution was adopted reciting the resent Apache outbreak in Arizona, and calling on the Secretary of War for information as to the number of United States soldiers now in the Territory, and whether the military force now stationed there is sufficient to grant full protection to the people, and also whether any legislation is necessary for the prompt and efficient security of the people against the destruction of life and property by hostile Indians.

In the Senate the Political Disability bill went over, and the Chinese bill was resumed, the question being upon concurring in the amendment striking out the Fifteenth Section which construes "Chinese laborers" to mean both "skilled and unskilled."

After Morgan and Call had finished speaking on the Chinese bill Pendleton maintained that it is the duty of Congress to put its interpretation of the word "laborers" in this bill, not only as a guidance for the officers who have to execute, also in the interest of the Chinese and all parties concerned. Edmunds remarked that ultimately the Chinese would have to decide the question and it would be just as difficult to determine the meaning of the words skilled and unskilled as of the word laborers. Collision at Sea.

SANDY HOOK, N. Y., April 28.—The steamship Nankin, from New York for Liverpool, was run into by the steamer Clyde this morning and lies in a sinking condition. The passengers were saved. The Clyde is badly damaged forwards.

A Ravisher Lynched.

ST. PAUL, Minn., April 28.—At an early hour this morning a party of masked men took Frank Warner, a trampaged 26 years, from jail, and lynched him. Warner was arrested on a charge of ravishing and brutally mutilating a little four year old girl. Before being hung he confessed the crime.

Hanged by a Mob.

FAIRVIEW, Ky., April 28.—At a logrolling here last Saturday, in a row, Bradford Courts, a young rough, killed James Smith and escaped. A posse of citizens followed him to Courts's house, where they found a large quantity of stolen goods. Courts and his brother William, who was also in the row, were taken to jail at Brookville. Last night a mob took them out and hung them.

LITTLE ROCK, April 28.—A Dallas special gives the particulars of the capture of the men who robbed the Texas Pacific train at Ranger station. The robbers were tracked by blood hounds into a canon near the Brazos river. A hot fight ensued, in which one of the robbers was killed, when his two companions surrendered. More of the robbers are at large with the Rangers in pursuit.

FORTRESS MONROE, April 28th.—The President and Cabinet had a brilliant reception here to-day by the sea and land forces. The North-German School ship Louise, from Havana, participated.

Against the Invasion.

St. Louis, Mo., April 28.—A large meeting was held at Lucas Market place to-night by Workingmen to express their sentiments on the Chinese question. Speeches were made by H. W. Williams, a prominent Greenbacker of this State, Richard Travelick of Detroit and Richard P. Parsons of Chicago, the general tenor of which was against Chinese cheap labor and Chinese immigration. Resolutions were adopted denouncing President Arthur for vetoing the Chinese bill, and characterizing his reasons for doing so as hypocritical.

WHAT THE JURY DID.
The Physicians Venture an Opinion- Various Testimonies-The Verdict.
At 9:30 yesterday Coroner Fairbairn held an inquest on the body of Frank McManus, at Warners undertaking rooms. The opening testimony was that of Wm. Gleason, who deposed: Am a police officer; saw body of the deceased; saw him last alive on Thursday night at 10 o'clock; arrested him on Thursday afternoon on complaint of some woman who said a scissors grinder had stolen a little girl; took a buggy went to the scene and arrested the man; took him to a store where he had purchased candy and the woman identified him as the man who had bought candy and brought the little girl away; took him to the police station; examined him and found blood on his hands, pants, drawers and vest; two fingers of his right hand were very bloody; he was locked up and a charge made on the book of rape; know he is the man I arrested and whose clothing was covered with blood; it was about fifteen minutes to four when I arrested him.

Chief A. S. Munger deposed: Am chief of police; knew the body of Frank McManus who was brought to the police station Thursday afternoon; removed him from the station Thursday night about 10:30 o'clock and placed him in the county jail in charge of the sheriff; had a conversation with the prisoner on Thursday night, together with Dr. Ames; he told me he met the girl with several others in front of a peanut stand, and gave her candy and then took her in a wood yard where he committed the crime; his body and clothing were covered with blood; this confession was made in the evening before he was taken to the jail; recognize the body as that of the man who was arrested and taken to the jail.

J. M. Eustis deponed: Am sheriff; the prisoner I recognize as the man brought to the jail by Chief Munger and Captain Berry on Thursday night about 10:30 o'clock; about 1 o'clock the next morning I was called to my door by persons who said they were friends, and demanded to be admitted; told them they could not get in that night; dressed and went to jail office just as the door was broken in; I was taken to a corner and held by four or five men whom I did not recognize; they were disguised; I saw hammers and timbers in the jail next morning, which I supposed they used to break down the doors; the man whose body I have seen is the man who was taken away; they took him away about 4 o'clock.

Officer Caswell deposed to seeing the body of deceased hanging to a tree on Fourth avenue south on Friday morning about 7 o'clock.

Dr. R. J. Hill judged from the appearance of the body that death resulted from strangulation by means of a rope, and Dr. A. R. Brackett concurred.

Jerry Murphy identified the body as that of Frank McManus, whom he had known in South Boston about eight years ago; saw him here two days after the election, knew that his parents lived in Boston in March last.

VERDICT,

STATE OF MINNESOTA,

County of Hennepin.

HOW IT WAS DONE.
Sheriff Eustice Did His Duty-The Supposed Security of the Jail.
To the Editor of the GLOBE:

The Pioneer Press contributor who signs himself "Luth Talger," is unquestionably one of those self-styled high moralists. He is one who broad-minded people call a "crank." In the face of the facts, as published in all the dailies, that Sheriff Eustice, even when seized with violent hands, jostled about, forced by a dozen masked men into a corner of his office, absolutely refused to give up the keys of the jail, and even when he was threatened with a fate similar to that experienced by the monster McManus, he bravely defied the vigilantes, saying: "My life is in your hands; you can take it but you will never get the prisoner from this jail." "Tell us where he is, or I cannot be responsible for your life," was the rejoinder, and rough hands were again laid upon him. "Never!" replied the sheriff, fighting and struggling desperately. Now this self styled moralist wishes the readers to understand that he, the immortal Luth. Talger, "was forced to believe that the sheriff of Hennepin county was highly direlict of his plain duty, at every cost, to protect the persons and lives of the criminals confided to his charge."

Your correspondent interviewed Matt Bross, for a long time the turnkey at the jail, and turnkey during the months in which the jail was reconstructed, upon the matter. He stated in most emphatic terms that when he learned the prisoner was to be placed in the murderers' row in the jail, he thought no lynching party could force down the various doors and take him out, even though they were suppiled with a full set of tools. The iron is so hard that no file nor chisel would cut it. Chief Munger was of the same opinion. To prevent bloodshed, no platoon of police was detailed to stand guard at the jail. The chief had every reason to believe that if there was a movement made to take out the prisoner, that move would be made by men of nerve, men who would not permit a squad of police to frustrate their purpose.
He also supposed he had every reason to believe that it was a physical impossibility to effect an entrance to the cell of the atrocious wretch by means of any ordinary tools. In regard to the former conclusion the chief was eminently correct. Had a dozen of the vigilants been shot down, fifty more would take their places, and a most bloody and desperate hand to hand struggle would undoubtedly have ensued. The chief acted rightly, and the sheriff's brave defense commends itself to every fair minded citizen. As your reporter stated in Saturday's issue of the GLOBE, the monster was not hung by a mob or rabble, but by law abiding citizens, men of influence, means and respectability—mostly heads of families, who had little daughters to protect. When murderers, and a thousand times worse than murderers, can escape the doom of the gallows through the damnable insanity dodge, then the people must mete out summary justice. LAW ABIDER.

St. Joseph, April 18—Intelligence was received here to-night of a horrible affair at Barnard, thirty miles from here. A tramp murdered a man named Alkire last night in cold blood. The citizens turned out and ran the tramp to cover, and found him entrenched securely in a lot of cord wood, where he could not be got at. They finally determined to blaze him out. Bottles filled with petroleum were pitched against the barricade, followed by lighted cotton. The heat ultimately forced the tramp out, and on his appearance was riddled with bullets, fifteen holes being found in him. No papers, letters or anything leading to his indentification were found. The man who gave his name as Cromley was found in cell No. 3 on the third tier. He showed the utmost nerve while he was being questioned by the vigilantes, making no effort to conceal his face and glibly answering the questions which were put to him. He told several conflicting stories convincing the committee that he was the man they believed him to be. To give him the benefit of whatever doubt existed, however, the attempt to break into the cell was renewed and proved successful. The prisoner was thereupon taken from the cell, securely handcuffed and the understanding made that if there was the least shadow of a doubt he should be returned to the jail. During all this operation and the events which followed the hardened wretch showed no sign of trepidation and was apparently as cool as the committee who were engaged in removing him. It was exactly 3:10 when he was brought into the corridor escorted by the entire company of vigilantes, the prisoner was marched up Fifth street to Seventh avenue, up Seventh avenue to Tenth street and thence to Fourth avenue and to the house of Mr. Spear. A sub-committee was appointed before leaving the jail, and had, when the prisoner arrived, called up Mrs. Snyder, Mrs. Smith, and Mrs. Powell, all of whom had seen the man prior to the commission of the crime, and gathered them at Mr. Spears'. No sooner was he presented than all the ladies declared positively that he was the culprit. The agonized mother exclaiming, "It is the man; take him away! take him away!" While this dramatic scene was going on in one room, the victim of the outrager's passion lay dying in an adjoining room. The positive identification of the villian by the ladies was the signal for action and without noise or any demonstration the prisoner was taken over to the corner of Fourth avenue and Twelfth street, and stood underneath a large oak tree on the south east corner of the block diagonally across from the High school. The noose was prepared in the most approved fashion with seven knots, one of the members of the committee climbing up and placing
THE ROPE OVER THE LIMB.

While this was in process of performance the prisoner was asked if he had anything to say and without the least sign of fear he replied that his name was Tim Cromley and that he was from Boston, and had been here four months. When asked if he had any parents, he said he had a mother, Nancy Ann Cromley, living in South Boston. He then took a member of the committee aside and had a moment's private conversation, reposing in him something to be delivered to to his mother at some future time. The wonderful nerve of the wretch still remained unshaken. When he was asked how he came to perpetrate the crime of which he was guilty. He denied it, but afterwards confessed and said it was done while he was drunk. His hands were thereupon tied behind him with a piece of the same rope procured for the hanging bee. The rope was then put over his neck and carefully adjusted under his right ear and at 3:57 with his hat and boots on he was swung into eternity the vigilants giving a long pull and a strong pull, which brought the wretch dangling in the air. The rope was then securely tied to the trunk of the tree. The grey dawn of morning was just breaking, and fully satisfied with the night's work the committee stood for a few moments watching the dangling remains, but unable, in the dim daylight, to detect the dying struggle (if struggle there were) of the victim of a speedy, retributive justice. While still standing gazing on the unusual spectacle a buggy drove up, there was a cry of police and the crowd rapidly and quietly separated. With the exception of some noise in the jail, the hanging was accomplished without noise or even loud talk, the whole affair, being manged despite the difficulty in getting at the prisoner with the utmost precision and best of order. The remains were left dangling in the air where crowds inspected them, as the news spread rapidly over the city to the early risers.

Negro Preacher Killed and Probably a White Man.
CHICAGO, July 17.—A special from Musick's Ferry, near St. Louis, reports that the negroes of that section are scandallized because Henry Francis, a German laborer, was living with an unmarried negress, and essayed to regulate matters. ADMIRAL SEYMOUR has issued a manifesto saying that he has undertaken, with the consent of the Egyptian Government, the restoration of order in Alexandria. A number of Arabi's soldiers were captured by marines and handed over to the Khedive, who ordered them shot by loyal troops. English sailors flogged ten Arabs who were guilty of arson, pillage, etc., and four men were publicly shot for murder, and one as a spy. The grain market has reopened, but hundreds of people are starving and houseless. Arabi Pasha is at Kafridwar, where he has four infantry regiments, 1,500 irregular troops, one cavalry regiment, thirty-six Krupp guns, and twelve mitrailleuses. He has been summoned to Alexandria by the Khedive, who will treat him as a rebel should he refuse to obey. Arabi says he did not intend to make war, but as the powers are determined to force an attack he considers it better to fight at once. He expresses willingness to return Alexandria if the Khedive will induce the English fleet and troops to withdraw. If the Khedive can not do this Arabi recommends him to send a minister to his camp and discuss the situation. A Constantinople dispatch states that Count Corti is strongly opposed to the Anglo-French control system in Egypt. Onon, representative of the Czar, is by no means kindly disposed toward the law of Egyptian liquidation which was established under the auspices of Sir Rivers Wilson. Baron Herschfeld, German representative, is known to favor the unrestricted military intervention of Turkey; this is quite opposed to the ideas of the Marquis de Noailles, and is against the traditional policy of France.

The United States Fish Commission has made a special report to Congress, which will be the most exhaustive work on food fishes ever printed. It will make three quarto volumes of eight hundred pages each, and be profusely illustrated.

STABBING HIS WIFE TO DEATH.
The Crime of a Laboring Man Which Was Witnessed by a Crowd.
Was Witnessed by a Crowd.

SYRACUSE, N. Y., July 9.—Great excitement was caused here this afternoon by a crowd of men, women and children following James Hawks, a dissolute laboring man, shouting: "Murderer! Murderer! Lynch him!" The police paid little attention at first, thinking he was crazy. In about half an hour the facts of a brutal murder reached the central portion of the city. Hawks and his wife, both about 45 years of age, had been drinking and Mrs. Hawks went out for a pail of lager beer. She stopped and had some conversation with two colored men, which so enraged her husband that he rushed out and stabbed her. She died instantly. The crowd who witnessed the crime followed Hawks for a number of blocks, crying at his heels. The police station was surrounded by an excited crowd, anxious to lynch the murderer. Hawks has been married four times and has been a terror to the neighborhood where he resided, commonly known as "Africa."
james-hawks-syracuse-1882-07-09.A3:
WIFE MURDER AT SYRACUSE.
SYRACUSE, N. Y., July 9.—This afternoon James Hawks, a laborer, stabbed and killed his wife in Grape-st. Mrs. Hawks had bought a pail of beer in a liquor shop and was returning home when she met her husband, who was intoxicated. Hawks drew a jackknife from his pocket and without a word stabbed his wife to the heart. He then threw the knife away and staggered up the street. The woman ran about thirty feet and clung to a tree outside the sidewalk. She died in about fifteen minutes. Hawks was arrested, and when informed that his wife was dead, exclaimed, "I am glad of it. It is a good thing for me."

Fire Bugs Rampant in Wyoming—Lynch Law to be Administered to the Fiends.

Railroad buildings, hotels and dwelling houses suffered alike. Vigilants have been patrolling the streets for three nights and have arrested about twenty strangers, but fires would start up on all sides. The prisoners were released. Dastardly Attempts to Burn the City of Laramie, Wyoming.
CHYENNE, Wy., March 22.—A reign of terror exists at Laramie City, fifty-six miles west of here. Incendiaries have been at work for four nights past, and fires have occurred every night, some of them being very costly. No distinction as to the class of property has been made, railroad buildings, hotels and dwellings suffering alike. Vigilants have been patrolling the streets for three nights, and have "run in" about twenty strangers, but the fires would start up on all sides. The prisoners were released. The terror is great because the people do not know what to expect next, for the reason that they do not know whom to suspect. There will be a necktie party if the offenders are caught.

The reported capture of the escaped prisoner Carter, who made his way out from the Rawlins jail at the time of the recent lynching, must have originated in an attempted capture made by deputies upon Wednesday last.

There is a place of very unsavory reputation about Rawlins known as the Hog ranch, and to this place several deputies went, getting wind of Carter's presence there. When they went into the house Carter escaped into the cellar. There the officers thought that their man was safe. However, while one of them was in the cellarway urging Carter to come up, the latter blazed away at him with a six shooter, the ball grazing the cheek of the officer, and the weapon being so close that his face was filled with powder. Value Must Be Attached.

New York, May 17.—The Times says the mining exchanges seem to be awakening to the fact that at least a suspicion of value must be attached to securities in which they deal, before the public will consent to place any confi-

dence in them. The American mining exchange has taken the initiative movement and it is promised they will develop soon into healthy proportions. In both exchange boards, long lines of stocks has been listed and dealt in of which few persons have known anything of a satisfactory nature. In fact it has been long notorious that mines which by sheriff sale, or more questionable means, have ceased to have any shadow of existence, were not only on the exchange list, but prompt in regular and irregular transactions. Thus was a premium placed on the corners and upon a long catalogue of swindles known best to adept mining stock manipulators. Striking such securities from the list of exchange has been advocated by prominent members, netably by President Smiley for a long time. The board of managers of the exchange heard arguments upon the matter a few days ago, and promptly determined to take decisive action.

The marshal, it is reported, would content himself with watching the Scythia. The Chester A. Arthur, with Pinkerton's detectives on board, was lying at quarantine at 1 a. m., but the authorities believe that the efforts of the New York police are merely precautionary and there is no real ground of suspicion that the Irish assassins are on board. The marshals have made a thorough search of the steamer Scythia, but found no assassins. They will also search the city to-day.

Terrible Tragedy.
We learn from various and reliable sources that Breaux Bridge was the scene of a terrible tragedy last Monday, and one in which unauthorized and unjustified violence held full sway. It appears that early on Monday morning a crowd of men—the number we did not learn—went to St. Martinsville and, by some means, took from the jail Joseph Jenkins, a white man, who was confined on the charge of having shot and killed his brother-in-law, one week before. Remonstrance from one or two persons, it does not appear that anything was done to frustrate the purpose of the mob, and the task of securing Jenkins was an easy one; there was also, at large and under bond, a negro man charged with the killing of a boy, he was likewise secured, and with the two the crowd returned to Breaux Bridge and there, in open day light, swung them into eternity.

Mob law at any time and under any circumstances is deplorable; if the circumstances of this instance are as we learn them, it is one of the worst cases of the kind in our State's history. It is said that justification of the act is sought in the charge of a flagrant and continuous neglect of duty on the part of the officers—especially of the Judge of that district. But even this could not justify, nor excuse such an act at this time. The remedy ought to be elsewhere, and when official incompetency or neglect of duty brings about such direful consequences, it is time for heroic remedies. If the district judge, sheriff, or any other officer be at fault, there ought to be some way of reaching them, if not, the district ought to be wiped out. We hope the Governor and legislature will give the matter some attention, since it is said by the friends of those implicated, that Jenkins and his fellow sufferer were victims, not so much of their own acts, as of a sacrifice to appease the wrath of an offended people.

Armed Negroes Swearing Vengeance in Louisiana.
Special by Telegraph to the Times-Star.]

BATON ROUGE, LA., May 25.—A perfect reign of terror exists in St Martin's parish, where Jenkins (white) and Ayroz (colored) were recently hanged by a mob of white men.

Ayroz's offence was so slight that he had been bailed out in the sum of $300. While riding down a road his horse collided with another horse coming from the oppositite direction, and the rider on the latter animal was thrown to the ground and the fall broke his neck. The fury of the mob was terrific. So anxious were the members of it to hurry Jenkins out of the world that they failed to tie his hands. The result was that when they suspended him by the neck he reached his hands above his head and grasped the rope. The crowd then rushed upon him and broke his arms with clubs. He then strangled to death and was left dangling in the air, with his unfortunate colored companion.

Some sixteen of the mob have been arrested. The negroes have armed themselves and sworn to be avenged for the unjust hanging of Ayroz, and a collision is expected.

THE LABOR PROBLEM.
The Trades Union people have to confront a delicate, if not difficult, problem in the unintermittent additions to the supply of skilled labor which Europe is now sending to the United States. Nearly every imaginable trade and handicraft now has its representatives among these new comers, and, what is more, they are men, as a rule, who are thorough masters of their trades, whatever those occupations may be, having served long apprenticeships to them at home, the periods thereof extending from five to seven years. At a time when a series of strikes for higher wages is in progress at nearly all our great manufacturing and business centers in the East, this extraordinary accretion of German, Scandinavian, Italian and British skilled workmen cannot but exercise ere long, if it does not already, a commanding influence upon the industrial situation. The comparatively insignificant wages for which this vast army of mechanics and artisans have been accustomed to to toil in the old country, make even the lowest wages here, against which our work-people are striking, very attractive, and it will be no easy matter, therefore, to persuade them to resist that attraction, in order simply to promote a strike. Thus far the Labor Bureau has managed to distribute them pretty well all over the country, so that the pressure at particular points is not felt, but it is believed that the time is coming when they will be concentrated in the cities, and become, as it were, a more compact power than at present. This is the contingency the leading men of the trades societies are anticipating, and they are preparing accordingly to deal with it. The first step is to secure the sympathies of the new comers, and with that view an endeavor will be made to reach them through the medium of circulars printed in the various languages, appealing to them, as a matter of self-interest, to make common cause with the workingmen of their adopted country, and thus secure the rights which were denied them under the tax-ridden, monopoly Governments of Europe, from whose oppressions they have fled. This work, it is understood, will be entered upon at once.

The country has a capacity of supporting a large population, and every mile of the length of the road and its branches will contribute to its earnings. A mob, five hundred strong, took a murderer named Jenkins out of jail and hanged him to a tree, his wife, who was among the spectators, pleading in vain for his life. Just then, among the interested bystanders, was discovered a colored man named Azar, who had shortly before been released on bail on a capital charge, because the Coroner's inquest showed that the homicide which he had committed was strictly in self-defense. But the mob's blood was up, and, almost before the bewildered Azar knew what was going

on, he was dangling and strangling by the side of Jenkius. It was a hideous piece of atrocity, and only worthy of the cowardly practices of Judge Lynch.

The scene at the jail passed off with an undisturbed calm except the efforts made by Col. Deblane, to dismade them from their illegal purposes. The young son of the Sheriff, who was acting jailor, and who saw that resis tance was vain, threw the key away and would be no party to the unlawful act. This double execution created a profound impression on the people. As we have before stated, the people were grumbling and their patience was well nigh spent; but still no one here was expecting this.
God forbid that we should make ourselves the apologists or try to palliate such illegal and violent acts. We do not recognize the right of any one to ap point himself Judge and take summary vengeance for imaginary or real wrongs. We do not acknowledge to any body of men, no matter how numerous or imposing it may be; the right of constituting itself a tribunal and condemn to death an accused person, without the hearing of his witnesses. A sudden ebullition, an indignation that leaves not a moment of reflection, only can palliate such an action, if such an action can be excused.

But this terrible drama, is not the result of want of reflection. An honest and peaceable population does not all of a sudden resort to reprehensible violence, without some powerful motive. There must have been hideous sores on the social and political body, for all honest element of the population, to be in such a state of desperation as to be stirred up and led to the perpetration of acts such as were witnessed here last Monday. The administration of justice in our parish, is but a cruel irony, but a cause of ruin. Our juries badly composed, badly constituted, do animated by prejudices, have made a comedy of the law and of justice, instead of being the safe guard of society invariably; in sectors of the law have been injured and this impunity has engendered a license so unruly that no one feels himself safe in person and property.

And the people crushed by taxes that disappear in the budget of criminal expenses, have risen in their might and eliminated those who have insulted it.

When it becomes necessary to resort to such means, it denotes a disorganisation in the political and social body and it can truly be said, that the decay arrives fast.

But while protesting against those acts, in the name of civilisation, in the name of humanity, in the name of the law; we hesitate to blame the people who, in their despair of seeing justice done, were forced to such unlawful means; but we do not hesitate to say, that our authorities are morally responsible for what has happened, in making no efforts and providing no means for the well being and safety of the people.—St. Martins Observer.

Sixteen persons have been arrested and imprisoned, without being allowed bail, in the St. Martinsville jail, for being implicated in the lynching of Jenkins and Azor. Feb. 21, 1882.

March is beginning to show her hand ahead of time. A regular hurricane prevailed through the whole of last night. The wind howled, and whistled, and screeched, till I began to think things generally were going to pieces. Considerable rain accompanied the wind. Four days in the past week without rain. Hurrah! Yesterday was warm to sultriness. The weather is still warm, and blowing a gale from the south west this morning. A little settled weather would be muchly enjoyed—even by this side-walk man.

I am not much of a believer in signs, but I wanted to tell the readers of the News last week of one I heard, but forgot to do so. The gentleman who told me of it, said he got it from an old lady twenty-five years ago; that he had no need it closely ever since, and has never known it to fail. It is this: If the 14th of February is a cloudy day, the fruit crop will be good. If it is cloudy half the day, there will only be half a crop. If the sun shines all day, there will be no fruit to speak of. A good fruit crop will prevail only in the section where it is cloudy on that day. E. G., in East Tenn., we have cloudy weather—plenty of fruit; in West Tenn., clear weather—no fruit. Last Tuesday was the 14th, and you will remember that it was a cloudy day. According to the sign we will have plenty of fruit. Make a note of it.

I hear of some narrow escapes, which occurred week before last, on the North Fork of Holston, during the prevalence of high water on that stream. On Friday the 10th inst., Mr. O. A. Rice started to ferry Dr. Martin, John Barker and Elias Littrell across the river at Ellington's Ford. The boat is drawn over by a rope stretched from one bank to the other. When the boat had gotten near the middle of the stream the swag of the rope caused the boat to dip water.—it soon filled and seemed to be in a sinking condition. The three passengers, becoming alarmed, jumped out. Mr. Luttrell succeeded in swimming ashore. G. bridge.—Dr. Martin, however, being lame, and not a strong swimmer, was in a perilous condition. Mr. Rice, seeing his situation, jumped out and finally got him safe ashore. Martin's Ferry was the scene last evening of a tragedy that for a time it was thought would result in the loss of two lives. About nine o'clock several pistol shots in rapid succession were heard in the neighborhood of the Mayor's office, and the sound of angry voices reached the ears of the people in that vicinity. A crowd gathered almost instantly from among which a stalwart negro emerged, brandishing a bloody razor, closely followed by Joe Bayless, and made his way up the Hanover street pavement. Just in front of Cott's grocery Bayless fell to the ground, saying that he was shot, when he was picked up and carried into Ong's drug store, the negro being allowed to go without blindrance.
At the Mayor's office, however, where the shots had been fired, an excited crowd gathered, and the word was passed around quickly that officer Wm. Linn had been killed by Otho Gilmore, the negro above mentioned, while the latter was being placed in the lock-up. In a moment several men appeared out of the crowd bearing Linn, who was covered with blood, which was flowing profusely from a murderous-looking gash in his left cheek. He was taken into Ong's drug store also, and medical assistance summoned. Drs. Blackford and Weirich were soon in charge of the wounded man, who was fairly gasping for his life, and prompt measures taken to ascertain his injuries and stop the flow of blood from his numerous wounds.
There was a gash in his left cheek, extending from his ear to his upper lip, and laying bare the bone; another near the top of his head, an inch and a half long, extending down toward his neck; and his hands were both badly lacerated, there being a severe gash just behind the left thumb, severing the tendons. The flow of blood from these wounds was very copious, and a large pool found on the floor. The crowd filled the store and it was with difficulty the doctors could attend to him properly; he was removed to the rear office, and the crowd excluded.

Bayless was found to have been shot in the right leg, just below the knee, the ball being imbedded in the bone, causing an itensely painful wound. He had also a cut on his right forearm and a gash along the knuckles of his right hand.

In the meantime Gilmore had been captured by Officer Wright, on Walnut street, near the Presbyterian church, and placed in the lockup. At first the report was circulate that he was in a dying condition, and that he had sent for his family, but this proved untrue. He had, however, been shot in two places, and the blood from a wound in his right cheek covered his face, making him appear as if frightfully hurt. The wound in his face was a slight one, however, the ball glancing from the bone and passing out an inch or so from where it entered. His severest wound was one in his right shoulder, the ball having pierced the collar bone, taking a course undetermined when our reporter left, but not supposed to be mortal, though severe.

The circumstances which gave rise to the affray are as follows: Gilmore had been arrested during the previous evening for disorderly conduct, for which he had been fined $3 and costs by Mayor Mitchell, and in default of payment had been locked up. During yesterday evening he had been allowed the liberty of the corridor around the cells, and between 5 and 6 o'clock made his escape by digging away the bricks from under one of the windows, which had been loosened by previous exploits of the same character. When this was discovered the officers went in pursuit of him, and about half-past eight he was caught near Burkhart's store in Seabright's addition by Officer Wm. Linn. Gilmore was brought down by the officer in his buggy, and before being placed behind the bars was subjected to the usual search.

The officer found a flask of whisky, partially filled, with which Gilmore was reluctant to part, and it was while taking this away from him that he began the assault upon the officer with his razor. Several men had in the meantime followed them into the front office, and when Linn came out of the lockup followed by Gilmore, he drew his revolver to defend himself, and began firing. Bayless attempted to thwart the blows of the negro, when LY27 received his cuts noted above. The officer found close range, and two of the shots took effect upon Gilmore as stated above, while one struck Bayless' leg. The officer and the negro clinched and fell to the floor, but the negro rose and made his way out, and Linn attempted to follow him, but he was bleeding so profusely from his murderous wounds that he fell at the doorway. Bayless followed the negro, in the attempt to catch him, but fell from the effect of the shot in his leg before he could overtake the fleeing culprit.

For a time the wildest excitement prevailed, and the report was current that Gilmore had murdered him. A vast crowd assembled in the vicinity, and for awhile there was talk of taking the negro and hanging him where he should be caught. When Officer Wright appeared with the negro the excitement ran high, and it was feared that he would be taken out and lynched, but better counsels prevailed, and he was locked up.

At eleven o'clock, when our reporter left, Officer Linn's condition was considered quite critical, though his wounds were not necessarily mortal. The severed arteries had all been caught, the flow of blood stopped, and he was resting easily, the physicians saying that unless something unlooked for happened he would pull through all right. Bayless' wound had been probed, and the extent of his injury found to be as stated above. Gilmore's wounds had not yet been dressed, but they were not considered to be of a dangerous character. In an interview he stated that he had not entertained any malice toward Officer Linn, but had used his weapon in defending himself against the officer, whom he alleged had assaulted him with his mace while placing him in the cooler. Gilmore is in the habit of getting drunk frequently, and is considered a dangerous man to meet when in that condition, though when sober is peaceable and industrious. When caught after, doing the cutting, he was making his way toward his home, and made no resistance to the officer. His wounds did not appear to be very serious as he was able to sit up and help himself.

A Drunken Negro, Perhaps Fatally Carves Officer Lynn and Joe Bayliss, Who Came to Assist Him—Account of the Butchery.

On Tuesday evening Otho Gilmore, a colored man of 45 years of age, was arrested for drunkenness and committed to the lock-up. Yesterday morning he was fined $3, and in default of payment was sent back behind the bars. Shortly after 6 o'clock, last evening, his cell was discovered empty and examination revealed the fact

HE HAD ESCAPED through the wall by means of an aperture, which, from the frequency with which it has furnished means of escape, is known as "that same old hole." An alarm was at once given and the police force sent upon a search for him. At 8;30 o'clock Officer William Lynn found him at John Burkhart's store, placed him under arrest and took him back to the City hall. In the Mayor's office he was searched and a half-pint flask of whiskey taken from him. During the search, Gilmore and Officer Lynn had some words and the negro grew abusive and insulting. In anguish Lynn, as he defended himself from the deadly attack, called out:

"MURDER! MURDER! HELP! HELP!"

After a moment, but not before a half dozen gaping gashes had been inflicted upon him, the officer got out his pistol and fired. Entering the room, he seized the now demoniac and infurated negro and, together, they fell to the floor. Officer Wright brought the demoniac negro to the jail and securely locked him up, while the two wounded men were carried into Ong's drug store.

were frequently heard. A strong guard was placed about the jail to prevent the administration of summary justice to the believed murderer.

In the meantime, a large medical force had been summoned to Ong's drug store to attend the wounded men. Drs. Warwick, Blackford, Hervey, Ong and Williams were present and did all in their power. Lynn was a frightful spectacle as he lay gasping there. Four gaping cuts were visible on his head and face and the hemorrhage of blood was terrible. A cut had severed the tendons of the right wrist and the left hand and arm had received two cuts. At a late hour this morning the flow of blood had been checked, but the life was in a precarious condition. Officer Lynn is a brave, good officer and very generally liked about the town.

BAYLISS' HURTS.

Bayliss was severely, though less seriously, hurt. The ball from Lynn's revolver had entered his right leg below the knee, and at last accounts it had not been found, though thoroughly probed for. He received two dangerous cuts on his left arm and one less severe on the right. He complained greatly of his stomach and had evidently received a frightful blow. His injuries are not necessarily fatal.

TWICE SHOT.

The negro Gilmore had been thrust into a cell and his injuries were left until the others had received attention. He was then found to be seriously injured. Two balls from Lynn's revolver had caught him, one dangerously. The first had pierced his right cheek, coming out at the ear, inflicting a severe but not dangerous wound. The second, received while he was on the floor, penetrated his right breast, breaking the collar bone and lodging in his body. The physicians thought the lungs had escaped, but could not, at this time, predict the result of the wound. Gilmore was slightly intoxicated at the time the fight began. He told a REGISTER reporter he "was not going to be imposed upon."

THE EXCITEMENT.

Scarcely anything in the history of Martin's Ferry has so excited her people. The immense crowd surged about Second street, in the vicinity of the tragedy, and for a time an appeal to Judge Lynch was imminent. Gilmore, who is the father of a family of six children, bears a rather unsavory reputation, while Lynn and Bayliss are both well liked. When it was learned Bayliss would no doubt recover, while Lynn had a fighting chance for life, the crowd cooled off, and, better council prevailing, decided to allow the law to take its course.

The latest information from Martin's Ferry, at 2 A. M., says the men are all in the same condition given above.

THE BUTCHERY VICTIMS.
Result of the Razor at Martin's Ferry- Lynn and Eayliss Will Recover and the Negro Will Probably Die.
Wednesday night's horrible butchery was the principal theme of conversation yesterday. The talk of lynching Gillmore has almost entirely abated and no trouble is anticipated. "We ought to hang the s—n of a b—h," and similar expressions are occasionally heard, but there is no fear of his being hanged. It now appears that lynching will be unnecessary, as Officer Lynn's second shot will end his career.

Joseph Bayless, the man shot in the right leg, was removed from Ong's drug store to this home on Second street early yesterday morning, where Dr. Hinerman assisted by Drs. West and Hobensack extracted the ball, which is from a 32-calibre revolver and weighed half a dram. The ball lodged between the tibia and fibula, about midway up the third chipping off a specula of bone from the fibula, and splitting the fibula two or three inches in length. The ball was extracted while Mr. Bayliss was under the influence of chloroform. He slept about two hours Wednesday night.

Gillmore rested very well after the wounds were dressed on Wednesday night. The second ball struck him on the sternum and turned to the right, its course then was directly under the clavicle passing backward, downward and slightly outward. The ball has not been exactly located, but from the way he complained his attendants are of the impression it lies near the upper portion of the shoulder blade, the ball not penetrating the lungs, at all. He rested comfortably during the morning, and all agreed in thinking there will be no doubts as to his recovery, so far as the course of the ball is concerned.

Gillmore has been taken up stairs in the City Hall, where a good breeze can be had.

Lynn was removed to his residence on Locust street. He appeared to be much prostrated from the loss of blood. Although serious, his wounds are not believed to be fatal.

The attendance of physicians is miscellaneous, Drs. Ong. West, Hinerman, Weirich, Blackford, Hervey, Hobensack and Williams rendering services. At a late hour, last night, Gillmore's condition was believed to be very serious. Some of the attendant physicians are of opinion he will die. The REGISTER's report of the butchery was much more acceptable to readers in Martin's Ferry than the account given in the Intelligencer.

otto-gilmore-martins-ferry-1882-07-26.A8: ON Wednesday evening of last week a very bloody shooting and cutting affray occurred in the lockup in Martin's Ferry, in which three men came very near losing their lives. It seems that a colored man named Otho Gilmore had been arrested on the previous evening on the charge of drunk and disorderly conduct, and fined $3 and costs, and in default was put in the lockup, from which he succeeded in making his escape on Wednesday. About 9 o'clock officer Wm. Linn re-arrested his man and returned him to the lockup without any trouble. Before putting him in the cell, however, he was searched and a bottle of liquor taken from his pocket, to which proceeding he took exceptions, when the officer reached for his mace, but before he succeeded in drawing it, the negro was upon him with a razor, the first cut laying Linn's face open from his car to his mouth. Several other serious gashes were inflicted, when the officer got out his revolver and commenced firing. During the fracas, Joseph Bayless and a number of other citizens had entered the room, and Bayless was attempting to protect the officer, and received several cuts from the murderous razor, and a severe kick in the abdomen. While Linn was shooting, the other two men were in close quarters, and one of his balls took effect in Bayless' knee; the negro was also seriously wounded in the shoulder. At first it was thought that both Linn and Bayless would die, and if such had been the case, we would most likely have had a lynching to record, as both are good and well-known citizens, and free talk was indulged in by the excited crowd which had gathered, about a rope and a lamp-post. At last reports it is thought that all the parties to the fracas will recover. Gilmore had a preliminary hearing before Mayor Mitchell on Monday, and was held in the sum of $1,000 for his appearance at court, and in default was brought to jail in this place on Tuesday.

An Insane Asylum Burned.

YANKTON (D. T.), April 3.—The Territorial Insane Asylum was burned yesterday. It was a temporary wooden building, used while the brick building, now nearly completed, was being constructed. There were 54 insane patients in the asylum, and of these the following were burned to death: Ossian Tverson of Yankton County; Peter Peterson of Cass County; Ivan Lynch of Union County, and Joseph Haverly of Lawrence County. The property loss is about $10,000, including a temporary building and its contents; insurance, $800. The origin of the fire is a mystery, and it was first seen in the roof. It spread with such rapidity that there was no time to save any property at all. The patients killed were once removed from the building, but ran back into the flames after escaping from the custody of their keepers.

A Row With Negroes.

Rockport (Mo.), April 3.—Some 20 or more drunken negroes created a disturbance on the streets late last night, and assaulted one or two white men. Several deputies were sworn in to maintain peace, who notified the negroes that they must disperse or be arrested. One of them attempted to strike one of the officers, who drew a weapon and fired at his assailant, but without hitting him. The negroes then fled, but some time later, and while some 15 or 20 men and boys were standing on the street talking together, a volley from guns and pistols was fired at them by the negroes from an alley on the opposite side of the street, and eight of the party were wounded, but none of them seriously. Great excitement ensued, and ten of the negroes were arrested and locked up.

Disabled Vessels.

HALIFAX, April 3.—The steamer Ayrshire, from Montrose, Scotland, for New York, with potatoes, has put in here, being short of coal. She had a most tempestuous voyage. The Captain had an arm broken, the carpenter a leg broken, and the boatswain a shoulder dislocated. The second officer was washed overboard, but a returning wave landed him again on the deck.

The Captain and crew of the brigantine William, wrecked on Sable Island, have arrived here. The vessel got jammed in the ice, their provisions gave out, and the men then subsisted 22 days on oats, which had been in the vessel two years. Water was obtained from pots in the ice.

Jesse James, the notorious train robber, was shot dead in St. Joseph, Mo., Monday morning. Since November last he has resided, with his wife, in a small shanty in the southeastern part of that city. Two of his gang, Robert and Charles Ford, have of late been living with him and arranging for a raid, which was to have commenced Monday evening. When Jesse laid off his belt to wash his hands, Robert Ford sprang up behind him and sent a bullet through his brain. The brothers at once surrendered to the authorities and announced themselves as detectives. James' shanty was almost an armory. A photograph of the dead robber was taken at the undertaker's. Dick Little was taken from Kansas City to identify Jesse, and recognized him at once. The wailing widow at last confessed that the corpse was that of Jesse James. There has been a standing reward of $50,000 for the bandit, dead or alive, and from mysterious hints thrown out by Governor Crittenden it is fair to presume that the raider was trapped by the state authorities. The mother of Jesse James reached St. Joseph Tuesday, and had an affecting meeting with the widow and children of the bandit. After viewing the corpse with streaming eyes, she was taken to the coroner's inquest. H. H. Craig, police commissioner of Kansas City, testified that Robert Ford acted under his instructions, but Charles was not commissioned. The jury held Robert Ford for killing Jesse James, and charged Charles with complicity. Mrs. Samuels, the mother of the out-law, created a sensation by a vigorous denunciation of Dick Little as a traitor. The remains will be handed over to her for interment. Robert Ford engaged as a detective in July last, and secured his brother's assistance. Bugler, one of the James gang now on trial at Independence, Mo., says that the Fords were in the Winston robbery. Governor Crittenden has sent five men to identify Jesse's body, when he will divide $50,-000 reward between the Fords and some officers who have worked up the destruction of the bandit.

THE LATEST FASHIONS IN LYNCHING
It seems that the administration of Lynch law is in these days of general progress being brought down to quite a fine point, and that when it is practiced most deliberately the effect is not much less impressive than that of a legal execution. For example, at Kokomo, in Indiana, on the 3d instant, a mob surrounded the jail where a man charged with an assault upon a child was confined, broke down the doors, took out the prisoner, and marched with him to a neighboring bridge. There the proceedings were opened in the most orthodox way, for the dispatch states that "the Rev. Mr. McClane was present and "offered a prayer." After the prayer had been offered the prisoner was invited to confess his guilt, whereupon he admitted that he had stolen a horse and a watch, but denied the graver charge. Then the mob mounted him on a box, tied his hands and legs, and asked him if he had any remarks to make. He responded by singing with great compcsure, "See that My Grave "is Kept Green." Whether the mob pledged itself to obey this injunction does not appear, but it would seem probable from the general thoughtfulness and consideration which it showed. The prisoner, having finished his hymn, and thus showed a somewhat classical taste in dying, like the fabled swan, in song, requested the crowd to hang him "decent," and this last wish was forthwith scrupulously carried out. The mob in this case appears to have been troubled with no sense of embarrassment, and to have gone about its work with a curious confidence in the legitimacy of its purpose. It may be judged from this that at Kokomo the practice of lynching has been kept up by frequent experiments, and it also follows that the regular process of the law in that part of Indiana must have fallen into contempt and distrust.
