John Burrows, living near Pittsboro, N. C., became deranged over the death of his wife and yesterday hanged himself from an apple tree.

During a fight yesterday at New York between Mrs. Douglass and Mrs. Kleinpiler the latter threw a broken lager-beer glass at her antagonist and struck a child and killed it.

At Belmont, Mo., on Friday night a sewing machine agent named Gardner was shot and fatally wounded by a man named Kilgour. The difficulty arose out of family affairs. Gardner died yesterday. Kilgour escaped.

There was a desperate encounter on Friday between Brown, the murderer of Deputy Sheriff Johnson, and an few rangers at Cibolo, Texas, a station on the International & Great Northern railway. Brown was killed and two men were wounded, one dangerously.

A Terrible Railway Accident.

An accident occurred on the St. Paul & Manitoba railway, 93 miles from St. Paul, causing the death of at least twelve persons, and doubtless others whose bodies have not been discovered. A work train of 22 cars, while running about eighteen miles an hour, jumped the track on an embankment about ten feet high, and rolled down into a pool of stagnant water eight feet deep. On the train were Swedish and Norwegian laborers. So far twelve dead bodies have been taken out and eight wounded, two mortally. The fireman was wounded but will recover. It is believed that more bodies will be recovered when the wreck is cleared. A special train with physicians and supplies has been sent to the place.

An Ex Soldier Meld for Murder.

In Baltimore Bernard McNally died from a sword wound inflicted by one of a party of colored men returning from Camp Argus on Wednesday evening last. Several of the members of Lincoln Post, G. A. R., were summoned to testify at the inquest, and, when they reached the police station, George H. Brightman, colored, vice commander of that post, was identified as the party who inflicted the wound. He had been described by several of those who were with McNally when the difficulty occurred. The jury rendered a verdict that McNally died of a sword wound inflicted by Brightman, and the coroner committed the accused to await the action of the grand jury on the charge of murder.

Men Scalded by a Boiler Explosion.

The boiler at the St. Catherine gold mine, located on the Air Line railroad, in the Western suburbs of Charlotte, N. C., exploded. Joe Roarke, white, and Abram Maxwell and Edward Wheeler, colored, the engineers, were terribly scalded. Roarke and Maxwell are fatally injured, the former having an arm and leg broken, besides being badly scalded, while the latter's head is perforated by a piece of the flying boiler and his side is cooked by the steam. Wheeler's hands were so badly injured that amputation will probably be necessary. Mr. Pitcher, the superintendent, was rescued from the debris unhurt.

Victims of Blasting Powder.

On the five mile section of the new railroad between Shamokin and Paxinos, on Friday last, a heavy charge of dualin was fired, causing considerable damage. Markle's beer brewery, in the neighborhood of where the blasting was done, was almost demolished. Sashes were broken and chimneys knocked down. A large rock struck a Hungarian on the foot, mangling his toes badly. Another laborer was knocked to the ground by the concussion. Superintendent Beddo states that the rock is like adamant, and that it takes an unusually large quantity of powder to blast it.

Alarming Spread of Scurvy.

Within the last few weeks thirty Hungarians and Poles, suffering from scurvy in its worst form, as well as pneumonia, have been admitted into the Schuylkill county hospital. The alarming increase of such cases has provoked much comment, and the matter will be laid before the doctors' association. The disease is ascribed to the almost exclusive use of salt meat by and the unclean habits of the imported laborers about the mines.

Fatal Freak of a Brooklyn Athlete.

William De Veer, aged 17 years, an athlete of Brooklyn, to amuse his companions, placed both of his feet at the back of his neck. He was taken ill afterward, and went to a physician. He, however, died, cerebro-spinal meningitis having set in. In accomplishing the athletic feat he had ruptured his abdomen and otherwise injured himself.

Fatal Accident to a Pleasure Party.

A coach in which a number of young people from San Francisco, who had been camping out in the vicinity, were taking a ride went over the turnpike bank, near Felton, killing the Misses Iva Cowdery, Eva Sussey, Celia Scott and Master George Scoot, and wounding Masters Burr, Benjamin, Beuling and William Moekles seriously. The accident was caused by the horses shying.

Maryland Affairs.
There were 244 deaths in Baltimore last week.
Eleven cases of small-pox were reported in Baltimore on Tuesday.
In one district of Harford county this season twelve self-binders were used.
The aphis or green fly has cut the rye crop short in portions of Harford county.
Immigration through Baltimore for the quarter ended June 30 was 18,584 persons.
The Fifth Maryland Regiment goes into camp at Cape May next Tuesday. The Regiment will be 300 strong.
The county tax in Charles county has been fixed at 95 cents on the $100, an increase of three cents on last year's rate.
John Price, of Abingdon district, Harford county, raised a Russian wheat this year, the heads of which were 7½ inches long.
Chas. H. Jenkins, of Louisville, Ky., won the fifty-mile bicycle race at Baltimore on Saturday. Time, 3 hours and 20 minutes.
The citizens of Frederick are arranging for a three days' jollification the latter part of August—military and firemen's parade, &c.
Congress has appropriated $20,000 to complete the survey for a ship canal to connect the waters of the Chesapeake and Delaware bays.
An Episcopal Church is to be built at Cresswell, Harford county, and A. B. Strasbaugh has donated a lot 90x120 feet upon which to erect it.
A reunion of the Lutheran ministers who were born in Middletown Valley, Frederick county, will be held at Middletown on the 26th and 27th insts.
Brightman, the colored Grand Army officer, has been induced for the murder of young McNally during the late encampment demonstration in Baltimore.
The Maryland Law University has filled the vacancy in its faculty, occasioned by the resignation of Colonel Charles Marshall, by the election of Mr. Thomas W. Hall.
The Baltimore & Ohio railroad has purchased the Cincinnati & Baltimore railroad, in Ohio, which will form an important link in the great Baltimore & Ohio system.
Miss Eliza Ross, daughter of Wm. J. Ross, a prominent lawyer of Frederick, was stricken with paralysis at the breakfast table last Sunday morning and died in the afternoon.
The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad has affected some extensive and important business arrangements in the West, and is double tracking the Pittsburg and Connellsville division.

The Frederick Riflemen, Linganore Guards and Border Guards, of Frederick county, and the Hagerstown Light Infantry will go to Cumberland on the 27th inst., on the occasion of the battalion encampment there.

The yield of wheat in Caroline county ranges from 15 to 25 bushels per acre. The yield in the aggregate, has increased ten-fold in the last ten years. The yield in Washington county is from 29 to 35 bushels per acre.

The Court of Appeals of Mazyland has decided that Mr. Somervell, the incumbent of the office of tobacco inspector of warehouse No. 2, is entitled to retain the office, there being no vacancy when the Governor appointed Mr. Smoot.

The Maryland Court of Appeals on Wednesday affirmed the order of the Circuit Court of Anue Arundel county refusing a mandamus to compel the comptroller to pay the annual endowment of $6,000 to the Maryland Agricultural College.

The engine of the steam threshing machine of James C. Tarbutton, of Talbot county, exploded Saturday whilst at work on the farm of W. P. Powell, and the engineer, a colored man named Lewis Conveye, was instantly killed, his body being blown a distance of 150 feet.

Wm. James Johnson was arrosted in Baltimore this week and committed for the action of the grand jury for having more wives than the law allows. At his hearing were two women he had married. He married one in Pennsylvania some years ago, and lived with her several years; the other he married in Baltimore last January. When arrested he was about to marry another woman on Bond street.

Mr. F. W. Pretzsch and Mr. John Able, of East Baltimore, matched two birds for a race from Washington to Baltimore on Sunday last. Mr. Pretzsch's bird, Bismarck, was liberated at 8.35 A. M., and reached home at 9.29 A. M.; time 54 minutes. Mr. Abel's bird was set free at 8.50 A. M., and arrived home at 10.15 A. M. Mr. Pretzsch claims that his bird beat the fastest time on record by three minutes.

An assignment by E. Steinfeld, in Rochester, New York, has involved the firm of Steinfeld & Keragood, doing business in Baltimore under the name of the Excelsior Clothing House. An injunction issued by Judge Dobbin has been served upon the Excelsior. The application alleges, among other things, extravagance in the conduct of the business in Baltimore. The liabilities of the Rochester house are said to be $50,000, including $26,000 in preferred creditors.

Mrs. Mary Bender, of Sharpsburg, Washington county, wife of Charles Bender and daughter of John Highberger, committed suicide Monday by swallowing a large dose of Paris green. She took the poison in the morning and then informed her husband of the fact. Medical aid was summoned, but the poison had taken effect, and she died at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. No reason is assigned for the suicide. Mrs. Bender was 22 years of age, and leaves one child.

Baltimore claims the best of free excursion societies. It furnishes one day's fresh air, two good meals, medical attention when needed, bathing facilities, and other enjoyments to 15,000 poor children every season. Every Thursday, 1,500 children are taken by boat to Chesterwood, a green retreat of a thousand shade trees. The supplies are bread in abundance, 200 gallons country milk, meat for sandwitches, 100 pounds of fresh butter, 200 gallons Java coffee, 100 gallons tea, and gingerbread, with music, and the cost comes within $400 for each excursion.

The vicinity of Fulton Station, on both sides of the Western Maryland Railroad, presents a busy scene. The new buildings of the Baltimore Car-Wheel Company, about 80 by 600 feet, are approaching completion, and the machinery is being put in. A large force of workmen are employed, and the work is being rapidly pushed forward. The Baltimore Paving Company's works, for the manufacture of compressed asphalt blocks, located north of the Western Maryland tracks, are also in an advanced state of construction. The main building is 50 by 75 feet, 33 feet high, with extensive shedding in the rear.

Business Failures.
NEW YORK, June 16th.—The business failures of the week reported to New York number 109, against 106 last week. The Eastern States had 13, Western 29, Southern 25, Middle 20. Pacific States and Territories 12, New York city and Brooklyn 10. The failures in New York, though numerous, are not heavy.

Killed by Lightning.
NASHVILLE, June 16th.—Lightning killed two men to-day. A fierce storm prevailed, which did much damage.

Accident on the New York Central Railroad.
ALBION (N. Y.), June 16th.—A wreck on the New York Central to-day killed two persons and badly shook up the entire passenger train.

Bonner Buys a Sister of Maud S.
NEW YORK, June 16th.—Robert Bonner has paid $12,000 for the filly Russell—a full sister to Vanderbilt's Maud S.

Assassination by Vigilantes
PARK STATION (Montana), June 16th.—Wm. Broder was called to the door of his saloon by vigilantes last night and riddled with bullets, because his place was a resort for thieves.

Independent Labor Party.
NEW YORK, June 16th.—The Independent Labor party was organized last night by the adoption of a platform that American mails be carried by American vessels; that "corners" in food and produce be prohibited, and opposing Chinese and convict labor. Vanderbilt and Gould, being in the opinion of the members largely interested in labor, will be invited to address the next meeting.

Beacon Park Races.
BOSTON, June 16th.—At Beacon Park yesterday, the race for the 2:38 class was won by Jack the Sailor, Previous second, Frank third. Best time, 2:35. In the race for the 2:29 class Clemmung was first, Pip second. Best time, 2:23.

Kenominated for Congress.
NEWCASTLE (Ind.), June 16th.—General Tom Brown has been renominated for Congress by the Republicans.

Defiance of Ex-Communication.
CLEVELAND, June 16th.—A picnic for the benefit of the Ladies' Land League was held yesterday, at which speeches were made encouraging the ladies to persist in their defiance of Bishop Gilmour's bull of excommunication.

Intimidation of Voters.
CHARLESTON (S. C.), June 16th.—Nine colored men have been arrested for intimidating and obstructing voters at the registration. A Supervisor was afterwards arrested for the same cause.

In order to let him die a natural death, the governor of New Mexico has respited for sixty days a murderer named Elijah Franklin.

MATRIMONIAL troubles covering a period of eight years led William Johnson, of Xenia, Ill., to kill himself and his wife with a revolver.

In the jail at Geneva, Illinois, Deputy Sheriff Lawson killed James Irwin for a savage assault upon him and an attempt to release twenty prisoners. The officer was promptly vindicated by a coroner's jury.

CYRUS CORRI, a wealthy farmer of Gratiot county, Michigan, threw himself before a train at Swan Creek and was beheaded.

The Providence pugilists, whose fight at Coney Island was recently interrupted, met at Fort Hamilton June 15 and had twenty-four rounds. Murrav was the victor, Greene being badly injured.

The increasing vigilance of the authorities at Pittsburgh prevented the Weedon-Maloney prize fight from taking place, but the principals hope to meet in the future.

At Park Station, Montana, William Broder was called to the door of his saloon by vigilants and riddled with bullets, because his place was a resort for thieves.

JAMES MITCHELL, of Mount Sterling, Ky., waylaid and outraged a farmer's wife and was jailed. Fye armed men took the offender from the officers and hanged him to a railroad trestle.

The Irish bishops have issued an address offering support to the people in peaceful agitation, and appealing to them to oppose secret societies as hostile to religion and to freedom. Evictions are pronounced permanently provocative of crime.

A DEPUTY marshal captured, at Carterville, Mo., three men who for the past year have been making spurious coin in a mining shaft. They had plaster-of-Paris molds for manufacturing gold or silver coin of any denomination. An accomplice was arrested at Carthage. Al pleaded guilty and were held for trial.

For five hours on Sunday there were bloody conflicts in the streets of Alexandria, between Egyptians and Europeans. Twenty persons were killed and a number of houses destroyed. The police were slow to interfere. Some of the wounded foreigners were taken to the French consulate, where riotous demonstrations soon took place. The English consul received a gun-shot wound, and the engineer of the British man-of-war, Superb, was killed. The military at last dispersed the rioters. The Greek consul and Italian vice-consul received serious injuries. A British vessel landed two hundred men to protect the consulate. The mob sacked the shops of Europeans.
